dgx_note: All 5 KR records (Bibimbap regional variants, competing origins, Obangsaek five colors, Jeonju Hanok Village, diaspora continuity) include data across four age tiers (pre-modern, early modern, modern, contemporary) and explicit epistemic classifications (folkloric, historical, culinary, architectural, sociocultural).

title.en: Bibimbap (Goldongban) & Regional Variants: Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong & Andong
title.fr: Le Bibimbap et ses variantes régionales : Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong et Andong
title.ar-LB: البيبيمباب الكوري وتنوعاته الإقليمية في جيونجو وجينجو وتونغيونغ وأندونغ
title.ko: 비빔밥(골동반)과 지역별 전통: 전주, 진주, 통영, 안동 헛제삿밥

records.summary: Explores Korea’s mixed-rice practice across Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong, and Andong, highlighting cooked, vegetarian, and allergy-safe options.
records.expanded_explanation: Recorded in late-Joseon culinary manuscripts such as the Siuijeonseo under the Hanja name goldongban (골동반, "mixed-up rice"), bibimbap unites warm rice with seasoned namul vegetables, sauces, and toppings tailored to local geography: Jeonju bibimbap uses broth-cooked rice, Kongnamul bean sprouts, and yellow hwangpomuk mung-bean jelly; Jinju features clam broth; coastal Tongyeong incorporates seaweeds and shellfish; and Andong Heotjesabap ("mock ancestral-rite rice") uses soy sauce instead of gochujang. For child safety and inclusivity, MiraVerse highlights cooked protein/tofu/mushroom toppings and sesame-free/soy-free options rather than raw beef (yukhoe) or raw egg.
records.time_period: Late Joseon Dynasty (19th Century Siuijeonseo) – Present

relationships.note: Regional diversity reflects multiple historical contexts

sensitivity_notes: Flag raw beef (yukhoe), raw egg yolk, sesame oil, and soy allergens; provide cooked mushroom/tofu vegetarian and allergen-safe virtual options for children.

age_tier_explanations.5-7: Arrange warm rice, crunchy bean sprouts, yellow mung-bean jelly, and cooked mushrooms into a colourful Jeonju bowl!
age_tier_explanations.8-10: Across Korea, different towns make bibimbap in their own way: Jeonju uses yellow mung-bean jelly and bean sprouts, Tongyeong adds ocean greens, and Andong seasons with mild soy sauce.
age_tier_explanations.11-13: Comparing Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong, and Andong bibimbap shows how local harvests—mountain greens, river plains, or coastal kelp—shape regional recipes and dietary adaptations.
age_tier_explanations.14-17: Textual attestation in late-Joseon cookbooks (Siuijeonseo’s goldongban) and regional specialization across Jeonju, Jinju, Tongyeong, and Andong demonstrate how a shared mixed-rice grammar adapts to local ecology and modern food-safety/allergen standards.

title.en: Competing Origin Narratives of Bibimbap: Ritual, Court, Agriculture & Lunar New Year
title.fr: Récits d’origine concurrents du Bibimbap : rituel, cour, agriculture et Nouvel An
title.ar-LB: الروايات المتعددة لنشأة البيبيمباب: الطقوس، البلاط، والزراعة
title.ko: 비빔밥 기원에 관한 여러 가설: 음복설, 궁중음식설, 농번기 들밥설, 섣달그믐설

records.summary: Presents four competing historical and folkloric theories for how bibimbap emerged, avoiding flattening them into a single origin claim.
records.expanded_explanation: Food historians identify at least four competing hypotheses for the origin of bibimbap: (1) the Eumbok (communal sharing of ceremonial food offerings after ancestral rites), (2) royal court cuisine (gungjung) lunch bowls, (3) practical agricultural field meals (nongbap) where farmers mixed side dishes into one bowl during harvest, and (4) Lunar New Year’s Eve (seotdal geumeum) traditions of mixing remaining winter side dishes before the new year. MiraVerse presents all four as plausible contributing practices rather than declaring one single unproven origin.

relationships.note: Multiple origin theories explain regional and social variety

sensitivity_notes: Never flatten competing origin hypotheses into a single historical fact; frame ritual theories as cultural history without requiring religious practice.

age_tier_explanations.5-7: Families, farmers in the fields, and festival guests all loved mixing colourful vegetables with warm rice in one bowl!
age_tier_explanations.8-10: Why did people start mixing rice and vegetables together? Some stories point to busy harvest picnics in the fields, while others point to New Year’s Eve family dinners.
age_tier_explanations.11-13: Food historians compare four different origin theories for bibimbap: harvest field meals, Lunar New Year’s Eve kitchen traditions, royal court lunches, and communal holiday sharing.
age_tier_explanations.14-17: Historiographical analysis of bibimbap rejects single-origin essentialism: Eumbok ritual sharing,农번기 (nongbeongi) agrarian field meals, courtly goldongban, and seotdal geumeum household practices likely converged into modern regional forms.

title.en: Obangsaek (오방색): Five-Color Cultural Symbolism & Harmony of the Bowl
title.fr: Obangsaek (오방색) : symbolisme culturel des cinq couleurs et harmonie du bol
title.ar-LB: أوبانغ سيك (الألوان الخمسة الكورية) وتناغم الطبق
title.ar-EG: رمزية الألوان الخمسة في الثقافة الكورية
title.ar-IQ: رمزية الألوان الخمسة في الثقافة الكورية
title.ko: 오방색(五方色)의 전통 문화 상징과 비빔밥의 조화

records.summary: Explains the traditional Korean five-color spectrum (Blue/Green, Red, Yellow, White, Black) as a cultural aesthetic and culinary philosophy.
records.expanded_explanation: Obangsaek (오방색, "five-direction colors") is a traditional Korean color system linking five hues with cardinal directions and seasons: Blue/Green (Cheong, East/Spring — spinach, cucumber, pine needles), Red (Jeok, South/Summer — carrots, jujube, gochujang), Yellow (Hwang, Center — hwangpomuk mung-bean jelly, pumpkin, cooked egg yolk), White (Baek, West/Autumn — rice, bean sprouts, radish), and Black/Dark (Heuk, North/Winter — shiitake mushrooms, bracken fern gosari, roasted seaweed gim). In MiraVerse, Obangsaek is taught strictly as an artistic and culinary tradition of visual balance, not as a universal scientific or medical law.
records.time_period: Traditional Korean Art & Culinary Heritage – Present

relationships.note: Color balance applied to Jeonju bowls and songpyeon

sensitivity_notes: Explicitly state that Obangsaek is a cultural design and culinary tradition, not a universal scientific or medical law.

age_tier_explanations.5-7: Sort five bright colours into the bowl: green spinach, red carrots, yellow jelly, white rice, and dark mushrooms!
age_tier_explanations.8-10: Korean cooks and artists use five traditional colours called Obangsaek—green/blue, red, yellow, white, and black—to make every bowl and hanbok look balanced and bright.
age_tier_explanations.11-13: In Korean cultural tradition, Obangsaek connects five colours (Blue/Green, Red, Yellow, White, Black) with directions and seasons, guiding how chefs arrange ingredients in Jeonju bibimbap and Chuseok songpyeon.
age_tier_explanations.14-17: Obangsaek reflects East Asian cosmological aesthetics applied to Korean textile, architectural (dancheong), and culinary arts—understood by historians as a symbolic cultural framework for visual and nutritional variety rather than empirical science.

title.en: Jeonju Hanok Village, Giwa Roofs, Nambu Market & Pungnammun Gate
title.fr: Village Hanok de Jeonju, toits Giwa, marché Nambu et porte Pungnammun
title.ar-LB: قرية الهانوك في جيونجو وسوق نامبو وبوابة بونغنامون

records.summary: Historic neighborhood in Jeonju preserving over 700 traditional giwa-tiled wooden hanok homes beside Nambu Market and Pungnammun Gate.
records.expanded_explanation: Located in Jeonju (North Jeolla Province, designated a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy), Jeonju Hanok Village clusters over 700 traditional Korean houses (hanok) featuring curved dark-gray giwa roof tiles, red pine pillars, breathable hanji mulberry-paper screens, and raised wooden maru verandas, near historic Gyeonggijeon Shrine, Pungnammun Gate, and Nambu Market. Real-world atlas markers distinguish public cultural sites from private residential hanok courtyards.
records.time_period: Joseon Era Foundations / Early 20th Century Hanok Cluster – Present

relationships.note: Culinary and architectural setting of Jeonju

sources.external_citation: UNESCO Creative Cities Network: Jeonju City of Gastronomy

sensitivity_notes: Respect resident privacy in living hanok neighborhoods; distinguish public landmarks (Gyeonggijeon, Pungnammun, Nambu Market) from fictional in-game family courtyards.

age_tier_explanations.5-7: Place curved dark roof tiles, sturdy pine wood pillars, and warm paper doors to care for Halmeoni’s cosy hanok courtyard!
age_tier_explanations.8-10: In Jeonju Hanok Village, hundreds of wooden homes with curved giwa roofs and paper screens stand near the busy Nambu Market and Pungnammun Gate.
age_tier_explanations.11-13: Hanok architecture balances nature and comfort: curved giwa tiles shed rain into courtyard drains, raised maru floors catch summer breezes, and hanji paper screens filter soft daylight.
age_tier_explanations.14-17: Jeonju Hanok Village illustrates urban heritage stewardship: maintaining over 700 timber-and-giwa structures alongside active civic spaces (Nambu Market, Pungnammun Gate) requires balancing tourism with resident privacy.

title.en: Shared Bowls, Chuseok Songpyeon & Korean Diaspora Cultural Continuity
title.fr: Bols partagés, Songpyeon de Chuseok et continuité de la diaspora coréenne
title.ar-LB: كعك السونغبيون وتواصل الأجيال في المهجر الكوري
title.ko: 추석 송편과 비빔밥이 잇는 한인 디아스포라의 세대 공감

records.summary: Connects Chuseok half-moon songpyeon steaming and communal bibimbap tables with intergenerational memory in Korea and the diaspora.
records.expanded_explanation: Shaping half-moon rice cakes (songpyeon) steamed over fresh pine needles during Chuseok and gathering around a shared table of bibimbap serve in Korean diaspora storytelling (including bibliographic candidates like Michelle Zauner’s Crying in H Mart) as powerful practices of family connection and adaptation when ingredients vary abroad.

relationships.note: Culminates in the Jeonju family courtyard celebration

sensitivity_notes: Adult NPCs operate the hot steamer; never collect personal family data from players; keep bibliographic references paraphrased.

age_tier_explanations.5-7: Fold half-moon songpyeon rice cakes over fragrant green pine needles and share a happy harvest feast in the garden!
age_tier_explanations.8-10: Whether in Jeonju or far away, families steam half-moon songpyeon over pine needles and share colourful bowls around the table to celebrate together.
age_tier_explanations.11-13: In Korean and diaspora households, preparing Chuseok songpyeon and adapting regional bibimbap ingredients keeps family stories and language alive across generations.
age_tier_explanations.14-17: Contemporary diaspora literature frames Korean foodways—from sourcing namul ingredients in expatriate grocery aisles to steaming Chuseok songpyeon—as living practices of cultural continuity and adaptation.
